section_summary: The section closes a January 1949 despatch on supplementary food rations for foreign nationals in Japan. Its enclosures present appeals from Kobe residents, comparative ration and price tables, French support, and a SCAP recommendation to end the supplementary rations. The final two documents concern a proposed fertilizer method that its advocates claimed could make Japan self-sufficient in food; officials found little support for the claim.

subfiles.title: Supplementary Food Rations for Foreign Nationals in Japan
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports consideration of ending supplementary rations for foreign nationals in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The concluding pages argue that the 1946 FEC policy did not require permanent supplementary rations. Officials feared extending them to Koreans and estimated the current program cost the United States about $728,510 annually. The mission suggests foreign governments could finance additional food for their nationals.

subfiles.title: Appeal for Adequate Food Rations for Foreign Residents
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Requests increased and more reliable food rations for occidental residents.
subfiles.summary: The committee says cuts to supplementary rations have left many long-term foreign residents unable to buy enough food. It compares their allotments with British rations, describes high prices and dependence on black markets, and requests more staple foods, dairy products, condiments, lower prices, and punctual distribution.

subfiles.title: Table A: Comparative Table of Basic and Supplementary Rations
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Compares foreign residents’ ration quantities across three periods from 1945 to late 1948.
subfiles.summary: Shows reductions in potatoes, butter, oil, and canned goods, alongside increased flour and newly allotted eggs.

subfiles.title: Table B: Comparison Between Present Rations for Occidentals in Japan and British Rations
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Compares monthly Japanese foreign-resident rations with British rations.
subfiles.summary: Lists quantities and unrestricted foods to support the committee’s claim that British supplies were more adequate.

subfiles.title: Table C: Staple Food Prices and Army Employees’ Salaries
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Tracks staple ration costs against approximate foreign-employee income from 1946 through 1948.
subfiles.summary: Shows rising prices for flour, potatoes, butter, oil, and sugar relative to salaries.

subfiles.title: Explanatory Letter to Heads of Diplomatic Missions
subfiles.to: Heads of diplomatic missions in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Seeks diplomatic support for the committee’s appeal over foreign residents’ food conditions.
subfiles.summary: The committee describes declining rations, inflation, inadequate wages, wartime hardship, and poverty among long-term foreign residents. It argues that many cannot obtain food through the Overseas Supply Store or open market. It proposes more varied official rations, relief for destitute residents, reasonable fuel supplies, and a way to purchase store goods using yen-converted dollars.

subfiles.title: Status of Foreign Nationals Residing in Japan
subfiles.about: Supports a fair resolution of the food-ration problems raised by the Kobe committee.
subfiles.summary: The French Mission endorses the committee’s concerns and favors fairer distribution of facilities for foreign nationals.

subfiles.title: Elimination of Supplementary Ration for Foreign Nationals
subfiles.from: Economic and Scientific Section, General Headquarters, Far East Command
subfiles.to: G-1, through Public Health and Welfare and Diplomatic Section
subfiles.about: Recommends ending supplementary food rations for foreign nationals on April 1, 1949.
subfiles.summary: The check sheet argues that food availability has improved since 1946 and that the original welfare measures were temporary. It estimates current supplementary rations cost $728,510 annually in imported food; extending them to about 600,000 Koreans could cost nearly $10 million more. It recommends ending the program while providing necessary free-market foods to indigent foreign nationals at Japanese government expense.

subfiles.title: Letter Concerning Fujimura’s Food-Production Proposal
subfiles.from: John M. Allison, Department of State
subfiles.about: Invites Agriculture officials to discuss Nobuo Fujimura’s proposed plant-culture technique.
subfiles.summary: Allison forwards the League’s summary and offers to arrange a meeting during Fujimura’s Washington visit.

subfiles.title: Increasing Japanese Food Production
subfiles.about: Records an interagency discussion of Fujimura’s fertilizer proposal and Japan’s food-production prospects.
subfiles.summary: Agriculture, Army, State, SCAP, and Japanese officials discuss Fujimura’s claim that a different fertilizer method could make Japan food self-sufficient. Agriculture and SCAP representatives find little technical merit and report that earlier Japanese and SCAP examinations reached similar conclusions. They also discuss the group’s aims and SCAP’s projection that other measures could raise Japanese food production by 15–20 percent by 1960.
